sources: Critical Vector — Ventilator Pocket Guide: Modes / Advanced Modes
Owens W. The Ventilator Book, 3rd ed
PROMIZING (Bosma KJ et al. NEJM 2025 — PAV+ vs PSV); NAVA meta-analysis (7 RCTs, 693 pts, 2021); APRV/BiVent meta-analysis (9 studies, 1,921 pts, 2026)

changelog.change: Initial entry — converted from the vent pocket guide: the three questions every mode answers, VC-vs-PC, the SIMV problem, the cross-manufacturer name table, and the adaptive/proportional modes with their trial evidence.

summary: Translate the mode name on the screen into physiology before you touch a setting. Every mode is a set of answers to three questions: what does the vent guarantee (volume / pressure / hybrid), who's in control (vent / patient / shared), and how does the breath end (time / flow / volume cycled). The mode matters far less than low VT, low Pplat, and appropriate PEEP.

items: What does the vent guarantee? Volume, pressure, or a hybrid — never truly both at once; one is always controlled, the other dependent.
Who's in control? Ventilator (mandatory), patient (spontaneous / assisted), or shared.
How does the breath end (cycle)? Time-cycled, flow-cycled, or volume-cycled.

rows: Set tidal volume is guaranteed; airway pressure varies with compliance and resistance. Consistent VT; barotrauma risk if compliance falls.
Set inspiratory pressure is guaranteed; VT varies with mechanics. Caps peak pressure; hypoventilation risk if compliance worsens.
A pressure-controlled breath that auto-adjusts pressure breath-to-breath to hit a target VT. Called PRVC, AC-VC+, AutoFlow, APVcmv, PCV-VG, POVAc by manufacturer.
Set mandatory breaths with spontaneous breaths permitted between. Largely supplanted by assist-control + pressure support (see below).
Every breath patient-triggered and pressure-limited, no backup rate. Comfortable and physiologic; unsafe without a reliable respiratory drive.
Two alternating pressure levels (Phigh / Plow) with spontaneous breathing throughout — preserves spontaneous ventilation and V/Q matching in ARDS.

body.text: VC vs PC is a non-debate: no RCT has shown a mortality difference; Cochrane found no difference in barotrauma, ventilator duration, or ICU stay. A PC-SV vs VC-AC ARDS comparison found no mortality difference (PC used less sedation). Protect the lung with the settings — low VT, Pplat < 30, appropriate PEEP — not the mode.

SIMV — the mode that won't die: between mandatory breaths the patient does ALL the work on unsupported spontaneous breaths unless PS is added, which can exhaust a sick patient and prolong weaning. A propensity-matched analysis (SIMV+PS vs assist-control, n=1,578) found no mortality difference and no measurable advantage. A structured SBT protocol does the weaning job more directly.

rows: Pplat from the prior conventional mode, not exceeding 30 cmH2O

Commonly 0 cmH2O — this does NOT create zero PEEP; the release is too brief for full emptying, so meaningful intrinsic PEEP persists. Raising Plow above 0 unpredictably raises both intrinsic PEEP and delivered VT.
4–6 s with reasonably preserved lungs; longer Thigh improves oxygenation
Most consequential, least standardised — commonly terminate the release at 50–75% of peak expiratory flow, targeting 10–14 releases/min

items: Hypercapnia → shorten Thigh (more releases), or lighten sedation to allow more spontaneous breathing (central to how APRV works). The brief Tlow release is the only point CO2 clears in bulk — very stiff lungs / high CO2 production make short release times hard to manage.

2026 meta-analysis (9 studies, 1,921 pts): APRV/BiVent improved oxygenation and increased ventilator-free days vs conventional ventilation — no mortality benefit. Treat any one centre's protocol as one implementation among several (TCAV personalises Tlow to the patient's flow curve — promising, unproven in large RCTs).

rows: You set a target VT; the vent delivers pressure-controlled breaths, adjusting pressure breath-to-breath to hit it (decelerating flow + volume guarantee)

17-study meta-analysis: lower peak pressures, better compliance vs pure VC in the OR (no ICU mortality data). Catch: a large spontaneous breath reads as improved compliance → the vent decreases support → potential under-support during high demand.
A specialised NG catheter senses diaphragm electrical activity (Edi); the vent delivers pressure proportional to it. PIP = NAVA level × (Edi max − Edi min) + PEEP

Best patient-ventilator synchrony of any mode (triggers off neural effort). Meta-analysis (7 RCTs, 693 pts): weaning success OR 1.93, MV duration −2.63 days, mortality OR 0.58. Needs the expensive proprietary catheter. Watch the Edi trend: falling as you raise the NAVA level = appropriate unloading.
Measures compliance/resistance in real time (brief occlusions ~q10–15 breaths), then amplifies the patient's own effort by a set % (70% gain = vent does 70% of the work)

PROMIZING (NEJM 2025, n=573): NO significant difference vs PSV in time to liberation, reintubation, VFDs, or 90-day mortality; less sedation (not prespecified). Clinicians frequently switched to PSV out of unfamiliarity. Works as designed, doesn't beat PSV when weaning is already protocolised.
Enter weight + target % minute ventilation; the vent uses the Otis equation to pick the VT/RR minimising calculated work of breathing. IntelliVent also auto-adjusts FiO2 and PEEP from SpO2/EtCO2
Shorter MV duration and lower peak pressures vs SIMV (pooled meta-analysis); no clear difference vs PSV for weaning. 'Black box' feel; Otis assumptions break down in complex ARDS.
